course.title: Design of Mechatronics and Robotics Systems I

lessons.title: What is mechatronics?
lessons.one_line: Mechatronics means designing mechanical, electronic and computer parts together, at the same time, so the product works as one smart system.
lessons.analogy: Think of a football team. Old-style design is like training the defenders, midfielders and attackers in separate camps, then meeting on match day. Mechatronic design trains them together from day one, so they pass better.
exam: Mechatronics is a methodology (a set of practices, procedures and rules) for the optimal design of electromechanical products.
It is multidisciplinary: electrical, mechanical, computer science and information technology.
It uses a concurrent (parallel) approach, not a sequential one, which gives more synergy.
It integrates electronics and computing with the mechanical system throughout the design process, giving more flexible, higher-performance products.
recall: Name two engineering fields you think a washing machine needs.
Why might building the motor first and the software later cause problems?

quiz.q: Which approach does mechatronic design use?
quiz.explain: Disciplines are designed at the same time, not one after another. That is what produces synergy.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the four fundamental disciplines named in the lecture?
quiz.explain: The four are electrical, mechanical, computer science and information technology.

quiz.q: A 'methodology' is best described as:
options: A collection of practices, procedures and rules
quiz.explain: That is the definition given on slide 3.

flashcards.back: A methodology for the optimal design of electromechanical products, combining mechanical, electrical, computer science and IT.
Concurrent: all disciplines designed together. Sequential: one after another. Mechatronics uses concurrent.
The combined result being better than the parts working separately.

theory.q: Define mechatronics.
points: A methodology for the optimal design of electromechanical products
Integrates mechanical, electrical, computer science and information technology

theory.q: What is meant by a methodology?
points: A collection of practices, procedures and rules
Used by those who work in a particular branch of knowledge or discipline

theory.q: List the four fundamental disciplines in a mechatronic system.
Explain the concurrent approach to mechatronic design.
points: All disciplines are designed at the same time, in parallel
It is not sequential, so one discipline does not wait for another
It gives more synergy and so a better product

theory.q: Differentiate between sequential and concurrent design.
State three benefits of the mechatronic approach to design.
points: Integrates electronics and computing with the mechanical system throughout design
Higher performance and a wider range of features

theory.q: Explain why mechatronics is called multidisciplinary.
points: It draws on several fields of engineering and science
Electrical, mechanical, computer science and IT
They are combined in one product, not designed separately

theory.q: Using a washing machine, show how a product has moved from traditional to mechatronic.
points: Older machines were manual and had to be used with care
Modern ones are smart and can be remotely operated
They use sensors, for example to detect motion

lessons.title: The mechatronic design toolkit
lessons.one_line: Engineers use software tools to model, simulate, test and even auto-generate code before building anything real.
lessons.analogy: It is like a flight simulator for engineers. You crash the virtual plane many times, cheaply, before touching a real one.
exam: Modelling: block diagrams or a visual interface to build easy-to-understand behavioural models of physical or abstract phenomena.
Simulation: numerical methods to solve models with differential, discrete, hybrid, partial and implicit nonlinear equations; needs a clock for real-time operation.
Project management: a database of project information and sub-models for reuse.
Design: numerical methods for constrained optimisation of performance functions; Monte Carlo capability is desirable.
Analysis: frequency-domain, time-domain and complex-domain design methods.
Real-time interface: a plug-in card replaces part of the model with real hardware (sensors and actuators). This is hardware-in-the-loop simulation or rapid prototyping.
Code generator: produces efficient high-level source code (usually C) from the block diagram, for the embedded processor.
Embedded processor interface: the processor that lives in the final product, and its communication with the prototyping environment.
recall: Why test a design on a computer before building it?

quiz.q: Replacing part of a simulated model with real sensors and actuators is called:
quiz.explain: Hardware-in-the-loop, also called rapid prototyping, must run in real time.

quiz.q: Which language does the code generator usually produce?
quiz.explain: The control code is usually C, compiled for the embedded processor.

quiz.q: A block-diagram tool for building behavioural models is part of:
quiz.explain: Modelling uses block diagrams or visual interfaces.

flashcards.back: Part of the model is replaced by real hardware via sensors and actuators, run in real time.

flashcards.front: What does the code generator do?
flashcards.back: Turns the block diagram into efficient high-level code, usually C, for the embedded processor.
The computer chip that sits inside the final product.

theory.q: List the eight tools in the mechatronic design toolkit.
Explain modelling in mechatronic design.
points: Block diagrams or a visual interface are used
Of physical or abstract phenomena, hiding complexity in sub-models

theory.q: Explain simulation in mechatronic design.
points: Handles differential, discrete, hybrid, partial and implicit nonlinear equations
Needs a clock for real-time operation and must run faster than real time

theory.q: What is hardware-in-the-loop simulation?
points: A plug-in card replaces part of the model with real hardware
It interfaces to actuators and sensors
Also called rapid prototyping, and must run in real time

theory.q: State the purpose of a code generator.
points: Produces efficient high-level source code from the block diagram
The code is compiled and used on the embedded processor

theory.q: Describe the embedded processor interface.
points: The embedded processor resides in the final product
The interface provides communication with the prototyping environment

theory.q: State the role of the design tool and of Monte Carlo capability.
points: Numerical methods for constrained optimisation of performance functions based on model parameters and signals

theory.q: Why should a design be modelled and simulated before it is built?
points: Mechatronic designs are finalised using modelling and simulation
Then prototyped and properly tested before deploying
Many trials can be run cheaply on a computer

lessons.title: Life-cycle design
lessons.one_line: Good mechatronic design cares about the product's whole life: getting it delivered, keeping it working, fixing it, upgrading it and disposing of it safely.
lessons.analogy: Buying a phone: you care how fast it arrives, whether it breaks, whether the screen can be repaired, whether it takes future updates, and where it goes when you are done.
exam: Life cycle design = producing high-quality products and maintaining them as well.
Delivery: time, cost and medium.
Reliability: failure rate, materials and tolerances.
Maintainability: modular design.
Serviceability: on-board diagnostics, prognostics and modular design.
Upgradeability: future compatibility with current designs.
Disposability: recycling and disposal of hazardous materials.
recall: List things that make a phone easy or hard to repair.

quiz.q: 'On-board diagnostics and prognostics' belong to which life-cycle factor?
quiz.explain: Serviceability covers diagnostics, prognostics and modular design.

quiz.q: Failure rate, materials and tolerances describe:
quiz.explain: Those are the reliability factors.

quiz.q: How many life-cycle factors does the lecture list?
quiz.explain: Delivery, reliability, maintainability, serviceability, upgradeability, disposability = 6.

flashcards.back: Delivery, Reliability, Maintainability, Serviceability, Upgradeability, Disposability (D-R-M-S-U-D).
Modular design.

theory.q: What is life cycle design?
List the six life cycle factors.
Explain reliability as a life cycle factor.
Explain maintainability.
points: So parts can be replaced and the product kept working

theory.q: What does serviceability involve?
Explain upgradeability.
points: So a product can be improved without replacing everything

theory.q: What does disposability cover?
What does delivery cover as a life cycle factor?

lessons.title: The 7 stages of designing a mechatronic system
lessons.one_line: Design is a chain: understand the need, study the problem, write the specification, generate ideas, pick the best, detail it, then draw it for manufacture.
lessons.analogy: Building a house: what the family needs, what is really wrong with the old one, a written brief, several sketches, choosing one, engineering details, then construction drawings.
exam: 1 The Need: starts from the customer's need, found by market research.
2 Analysis of the problem: the critical stage. Find the true nature of the problem or the design wastes time.
3 Specification: mass, dimensions, accuracy, I/O, interfaces, power, environment, standards, space, payload, speed, acceleration, resolution, control functions, life.
4 Conceptualisation: generate possible solutions for each function; aim for at least six per function.
5 Optimisation: pick the best solution from the group.
6 Detail design: prototype, mechanical layout, check components fit and can be accessed for maintenance.
7 Production of working drawings: drawings, circuit diagrams and manufacturing tolerances.
recall: Why is writing a specification before designing a good idea?

quiz.q: Which stage is called the critical stage?
quiz.explain: Wrongly defining the problem wastes time and may not meet the need.

quiz.q: Choosing the best solution among several is:
quiz.explain: Optimisation = selecting the best solution from a group.

quiz.q: Manufacturing tolerances are included in:
quiz.explain: Working drawings include the tolerance for each component.

quiz.q: Roughly how many solutions should you try to think of per function?
quiz.explain: Slide 17 says at least six.

flashcards.back: Need, Analysis, Specification, Conceptualisation, Optimisation, Detail design, Working drawings.
Mass, dimensions, accuracy, I/O, interfaces, power, environment, standards, space, payload, speed, life etc.
That all components physically fit and can be reached for replacement or maintenance.

theory.q: List the seven stages of designing a mechatronic system in order.
Explain why analysis of the problem is the critical stage.
points: It finds the true nature of the problem
A wrongly defined problem wastes time
The design may then fail to meet the need

theory.q: Explain the first stage, the need.
points: Design starts from the need of a customer
Failures are more common at this stage

theory.q: List six items that may appear in a specification.
Explain conceptualisation.
points: Possible solutions are generated for each function
Think of at least six for each function
Use similar solved problems or new techniques

theory.q: Define optimisation in design.
points: A technique in which the best solution is selected from a group
The solutions are evaluated and the most suitable is chosen

theory.q: What is done during detail design?
points: The chosen solution is developed in detail, for example a prototype
The mechanical layout is made so components physically fit
Components must be accessible for replacement and maintenance

theory.q: What do the working drawings contain?
points: The selected design translated into working drawings and circuit diagrams
So the item can be made

lessons.title: Traditional vs mechatronics approach
lessons.one_line: Traditional machines are big, mechanical and fixed; mechatronic machines are compact, sensor-driven and programmable.
lessons.analogy: An old manual typewriter versus a laptop: one is heavy and fixed, the other is light and does far more, but costs more.
exam: Traditional: bulk, manual control, complex mechanism, non-adjustable cycles, constant-speed drives, mechanical synchronisation, accuracy set by mechanism tolerance, more components, rigid heavy structure, less accuracy, less flexibility, lower cost.

Mechatronics: compact, microprocessor/controller control, simplified mechanism, programmed movements, variable-speed drives, electronic synchronisation, accuracy by feedback, fewer components, light structure, more accurate, more flexible, higher cost.
Traditional systems are finalised by iterating design equations and numerical analysis; mechatronic systems by modelling, simulation and prototyping.
Washing machine example: manual and cautious before; smart, sensor-based and remote now.
recall: What extra thing does a modern washing machine have that an old one lacks?

quiz.q: In mechatronics, accuracy is achieved mainly by:
quiz.explain: Traditional relies on mechanism tolerance; mechatronics on feedback.

quiz.q: Which is a drawback of the mechatronics approach?
quiz.explain: Cost is the one row where mechatronics is worse.

quiz.q: Synchronisation in mechatronics is:
quiz.explain: Traditional = mechanical; mechatronic = electronic.

flashcards.back: Constant-speed vs variable-speed.
Cost: traditional is cheaper.
By microprocessor or controller.

theory.q: State five differences between the traditional and mechatronic approaches.
points: Non-adjustable movement cycles versus programmed movements

theory.q: How is accuracy achieved in each approach?
points: Traditional: determined by the tolerance of the mechanism
So mechatronic systems are more accurate

theory.q: Compare how each approach achieves synchronisation.
Compare structure and number of components in the two approaches.
points: Mechatronic has fewer components and a light structure

theory.q: State one disadvantage of the mechatronic approach.
How is a design finalised in each approach?
points: Traditional: iterations of design equations and numerical analysis
Mechatronic: modelling and simulation, then prototyping

theory.q: Use the washing machine to illustrate the mechatronic approach.
points: Old machines were manual and used with precautions
New ones are smart and remotely operated
They use sensors and a controller, with simple mechanisms and fewer moving parts

theory.q: Why are mechatronic systems more flexible?
points: Movements are programmed and can be changed

lessons.title: Case study: Pick and place robot
lessons.one_line: A robot that picks an object up and puts it somewhere else, using pneumatic cylinders, limit switches and a microcontroller.
lessons.analogy: A claw-machine arm at an arcade: rotate, reach, drop down, close the grip, lift, move, release.
exam: Configurations: cylindrical, spherical, articulated or SCARA.
Parts: manipulator/arm (called 'rover' in the slides), end effector, actuators (servo, stepper, pneumatic or hydraulic), sensors (touch, IR), controller.
Movements: base rotates CW and CCW; arm extends and retracts; arm moves up and down; gripper opens and closes.
Driven by pneumatic cylinders operated by solenoid valves, with limit switches to signal completed motions.
Microcontroller (M68HC11 family) senses 8 limit switches on Port C (PC0-PC7), a start/stop line on Port D, and drives 8 movements on Port B (PB0-PB7).
Each output drives a TRIAC opto-isolator (LED + TRIAC) that switches the solenoid valve supply.
Advantages: fast, flexible, accurate, safer, never tired. Uses: defence, industry, medicine.
recall: Which body part does an end effector copy?

quiz.q: What tells the controller a movement is finished?
quiz.explain: Limit switches indicate motion completion.

quiz.q: Which port senses the limit switches?
quiz.explain: PC0-PC7 read eight limit switches.

quiz.q: What isolates the microcontroller from the solenoid supply?
quiz.explain: An LED + TRIAC pair gives electrical isolation.

quiz.q: The gripper is the:
quiz.explain: The end effector is attached to the last joint and grips objects.

flashcards.back: Manipulator, end effector, actuators, sensors, controller.
Sends 8 output signals for the 8 movements.
To protect the microcontroller from the higher-power solenoid circuit.

theory.q: What is a pick and place robot?
points: A robot used to pick up an object
And place it in the desired location

theory.q: List the main parts of a pick and place robot and state the function of each.
points: Manipulator or arm: the main body of rigid links and joints
End effector: grips or handles objects, like a hand
Actuators: the drivers, for example servo, stepper, pneumatic or hydraulic
Sensors: sense internal and external state, for example touch or IR
Controller: controls the actuators from sensor feedback

theory.q: List the four movements of the robot.
points: Clockwise and anticlockwise rotation of the base
Horizontal movement of the arm: extend or retract
Up and down movement of the arm
Open or close movement of the gripper

theory.q: Explain how the movements are produced.
points: Limit switches indicate when a motion is completed

theory.q: State the function of Port B, Port C and Port D of the microcontroller.
points: Port C (PC0 to PC7) senses eight limit switches
Port B (PB0 to PB7) controls the eight movements
A Port D line starts or stops the robot

theory.q: Explain the role of the TRIAC opto-isolator.
points: It consists of an LED and a TRIAC
It isolates the microcontroller from the solenoid supply
It regulates the supply to the solenoid valve that operates the piston

theory.q: Give four advantages of pick and place robots.
points: Safer working environment and never tired

theory.q: State three application areas of pick and place robots.
points: Defence: for example surveillance or diffusing bombs
Industry: moving parts to a machine or conveyor

lessons.title: Case study: Engine management system (EMS)
lessons.one_line: The engine's brain: sensors read what the engine is doing, a microcontroller decides, and drivers adjust fuel and spark.
lessons.analogy: Like a driver who feels speed, heat and airflow and adjusts pedal and gears instantly, but done thousands of times a second.
exam: EMS = sensors, relays, actuators and an Engine Control Unit (ECU). Used with MPFI, GDI (petrol) and CRDi (diesel).
Controls ignition and fuelling; goal is optimum engine settings, more efficient and less polluting.
Power and speed are controlled by varying ignition timing and air-fuel mixture.
Timing wheel gives pulses showing crankshaft position; the microprocessor times high-voltage pulses accordingly.
Fuel amount comes from a mass air flow sensor input; injector valve time is varied.
Sensors: engine speed (inductive coil + toothed wheel), temperature (thermistor or thermocouple), hot-wire anemometer (mass airflow), oxygen sensor (zirconia tube, works above ~300 degrees C).
Chain: sensors, signal conditioning, ADC, microcontroller compares with stored set points, drivers, actuators.
Transient protection circuit guards against supply surges; a voltage regulator supplies the controller.
Advantages: good acceleration, idle speed control, cruise control, self-diagnosis, lower fuel use, safety.
recall: What two things does an engine need mixed and lit to run?

quiz.q: Which sensor uses a heated wire cooled by air?
quiz.explain: The cooling depends on mass flow rate of air.

quiz.q: Analog sensor signals are converted for the microcontroller by:
quiz.explain: ADC = analog to digital.

quiz.q: The oxygen sensor's electrolyte is made of:
quiz.explain: A closed-end zirconia tube with porous platinum electrodes.

quiz.q: What does the timing wheel produce?
quiz.explain: Those pulses let the microprocessor time the spark.

flashcards.back: Sensors + ECU + actuators controlling fuel and ignition for optimum performance.
Sensor, conditioning, ADC, microcontroller, driver, actuator.

flashcards.front: Two variables that set engine power?
flashcards.back: Ignition timing and air-fuel mixture.

theory.q: What does EMS stand for, and what is it?
points: Electronic and electrical components such as sensors, relays, actuators and an Engine Control Unit

theory.q: List the main components of an EMS.
State the main objective of an engine management system.
points: To operate the engine at its optimum settings
Making the combustion process more efficient and less polluting

theory.q: How are engine power and speed controlled?
points: This is done by a microprocessor in modern cars

theory.q: Explain how ignition timing is controlled.
points: The crankshaft drives a distributor and a timing wheel
The timing wheel generates pulses showing crankshaft position
The microprocessor adjusts when high-voltage pulses are sent
So sparks occur at the right moment

theory.q: Explain how the amount of fuel injected is determined.
points: From the mass air flow sensor input, or computed from other measurements
The microprocessor outputs a signal to the fuel injector valve
The injector valve open time is varied

theory.q: Describe any three sensors used in an EMS.
points: Engine speed: inductive coil and toothed wheel
Mass air flow: hot-wire anemometer, cooled by air flow
Oxygen: zirconia tube with platinum electrodes, works above about 300 degrees C
Throttle position sensor (any three, with how each works)

theory.q: Describe the signal chain from sensors to actuators.
points: Signal conditioning prepares the signals and an ADC digitises them
The microcontroller compares with stored set points
Drivers act on the output signals to operate the actuators

lessons.title: Case study: Automatic car park barrier
lessons.one_line: Coin in, entrance barrier up; car at the exit, exit barrier up. Solenoid valves and a PLC do the switching.
lessons.analogy: An automatic gate that opens only when it hears the right 'password' (a coin or a car).
exam: Entry barrier opens when the correct coin is inserted; exit barrier opens when a car is detected at the exit.
Current through solenoid A extends the piston, rotating the barrier up. When current stops, the valve spring returns it. Current through solenoid B moves the piston down.
Limit switches detect barrier fully up and fully down.
PLC has 6 inputs (X400-X405): coin switch, entrance up, entrance down, car at exit, exit up, exit down; 4 outputs (Y430-Y433): solenoids A and B for entrance and exit barriers.
Inputs give 0 V when a switch is operated and +24 V otherwise.
recall: Why would a barrier need to know it has reached the top?

quiz.q: How many PLC inputs does the system use?
Solenoid B on the entrance valve does what?
quiz.explain: A raises, B lowers.

quiz.q: Which triggers the exit barrier?
quiz.explain: The car-at-exit switch (X403).

flashcards.back: Drive solenoids A and B for both barriers.
Detect barrier fully up or down.
0 V when switch operated, +24 V otherwise.

theory.q: Describe how the entrance barrier of the car park works.
points: The correct coin inserted operates the coin switch
Current flows through solenoid A, extending the piston

theory.q: What causes the exit barrier to open?
points: A car is detected at the exit
The exit barrier is then raised

theory.q: State the role of the limit switches in the system.
points: They detect the barrier fully up
They detect the barrier fully down

theory.q: State the inputs and outputs of the PLC used.
points: Coin switch, entrance up, entrance down
Car at exit, exit up, exit down
Four outputs, Y430 to Y433: solenoids A and B for entrance and exit

theory.q: Explain the roles of solenoid A and solenoid B on the valve.
points: Current through A extends the piston and raises the barrier
Current through B moves the piston down and lowers the barrier
When current stops the valve spring returns the valve

theory.q: State the input voltage convention used.
points: 0 V when a switch is operated

theory.q: What does the PLC do in this system?
points: Drives the solenoid outputs in the programmed sequence

theory.q: Describe the sequence from coin insertion to the barrier closing.
points: Solenoid A energised and barrier rises
Solenoid B lowers the barrier, entrance down limit switch confirms

lessons.title: What is automation and why do it?
lessons.one_line: Automation means letting machines run a process with as little human effort as possible.
lessons.analogy: A traffic light that changes by itself instead of a police officer waving cars through.
exam: Automation: a process to create, control and monitor technology applications; operating equipment (machinery, ships' stabilisation, aircraft, boilers) with minimum human effort.

Reasons: raise labour productivity, cut labour cost, ease labour shortages, remove routine manual and clerical tasks, improve worker safety, improve product quality, cut manufacturing lead time, do processes impossible manually, avoid the high cost of not automating.
Major industrial areas: transporting, working (processing) and packaging.
recall: Name a job in Nigeria that a machine could do more safely than a person.

quiz.q: Which is a reason for automation?
quiz.explain: Safety, quality, productivity and lower lead time are all reasons.

quiz.q: Automation aims for:
quiz.explain: That is the core definition.

quiz.q: Which is NOT one of the three major automation areas listed?
quiz.explain: The lecture lists transporting, working and packaging.

flashcards.back: Running equipment or processes with minimum human effort.
Time from starting a product's production to finishing it. Automation reduces it.

theory.q: Define automation.
points: A process to create, control and monitor technology applications
Operating equipment with minimum human effort

theory.q: State five reasons for automation.
points: Remove routine manual and clerical tasks

theory.q: List the three major industrial areas of automation.
Explain how automation improves safety and quality.
points: Machines take over routine and hazardous manual tasks
Product quality improves through consistent operation

theory.q: What is manufacturing lead time?
points: The time from starting a product's production to finishing it

theory.q: Give examples of equipment that can be automated.
Explain the reason 'avoid the high cost of not automating'.
points: Staying manual can cost more in labour, time and quality
So automation can be the cheaper long-term choice

theory.q: Explain two ways automation helps with labour.

lessons.title: Fixed, programmable and flexible automation
lessons.one_line: Fixed is built for one job at high volume; programmable handles batches; flexible switches products without stopping.
lessons.analogy: Fixed: a bottling line that only fills one bottle. Programmable: a bakery oven you reset between bread types. Flexible: a kitchen that cooks different orders at the same time.
exam: Fixed (hard) automation: hardware-based, cannot be changed; high demand, long product life; max efficiency, lowest unit cost; large initial investment, inflexible.
Programmable automation: hardware + software; batch production; flexible to product changes; low unit cost for large batches; long set-up time for new products; higher unit cost than fixed.

Flexible automation (FMS / CIM): programmable but changeover without stopping; several products at once; low volume, varying demand, short life cycles; customised products; large investment, high unit cost.
Example of flexible: automobile assembly line.
recall: Which is cheapest per item if you make millions of one thing?

quiz.q: Best choice for very high volume and a long product life?
quiz.explain: Fixed gives maximum efficiency and lowest unit cost at high volume.

quiz.q: FMS stands for:
quiz.explain: It is another name for flexible automation.

quiz.q: Long set-up time for a new product is a weakness of:
quiz.explain: Programmable needs reprogramming and set-up between batches.

quiz.q: Which suits short product life cycles and customised items?
quiz.explain: Flexible copes with design variation.

flashcards.back: Max efficiency, low unit cost. Large investment, inflexible.
Batch production, products with different options.
Low rates, varying demand, short life cycles, customised products.

theory.q: Define fixed (hard) automation.
State two advantages and two disadvantages of fixed automation.
points: Advantage: lowest unit cost at high volume

theory.q: Describe programmable automation and where it is used.
points: Can be reprogrammed for product changes

theory.q: Explain flexible automation and give an example.
points: An automobile assembly line is an example

theory.q: Compare fixed and flexible automation.
points: Fixed: high volume, one product; flexible: low volume, varied products
Fixed: lowest unit cost; flexible: high unit cost
Fixed: inflexible; flexible: handles design variation
Fixed: large investment; flexible: also large investment

theory.q: State two disadvantages of programmable automation.
points: Long set-up time for a new product

theory.q: Which type suits short product life cycles and customised products, and why?
points: It handles low volume and varying demand

theory.q: What do FMS and CIM stand for?

lessons.title: What is a robot? What is robotics?
lessons.one_line: A robot is a reprogrammable machine with links, joints and motors that moves things through programmed motion. Robotics is the field of designing and using them.
lessons.analogy: Your arm: bones are links, elbows are joints, muscles are actuators, brain is the controller.
exam: 'Robot' coined by Karel Capek in the 1920 play R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots); Czech for worker/servant.
Manipulator = series of links connected by joints, each with an actuator; one end on a stable base, the other holds a tool.
RIA definition: re-programmable, multifunctional manipulator moving material, parts, tools or devices through variable programmed motion for a variety of tasks.
Japanese definition: all-purpose machine with a memory device that can replace human labour for automatic performance of tasks.
Schilling: software-controlled mechanical device using sensors to guide end effectors through programmed motions in a workspace to manipulate objects.
Robotics: art, knowledge base and know-how of designing, applying and using robots; interdisciplinary.
recall: What does 'reprogrammable' add compared to a toy that does one motion?

quiz.q: Who coined the word 'robot'?
quiz.explain: In the 1920 play R.U.R.

quiz.q: Links are connected by:
quiz.explain: Each joint usually has an actuator.

quiz.q: 'Reprogrammable' in the RIA definition means:
options: Motion can be changed by reprogramming
quiz.explain: That separates robots from fixed automation.

flashcards.back: Czech for worker/servant; Karel Capek, R.U.R., 1920.
A chain of links and joints, with actuators, between a base and a tool.
Designing, applying and using robots; interdisciplinary.

theory.q: State the origin of the word 'robot'.
points: In the 1920 play R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots)

theory.q: Define a manipulator.
points: A series of links connected by joints, each with an actuator
One end on a stable base, the other holding a tool

theory.q: State the RIA definition of a robot.
points: Moves material, parts, tools or devices

theory.q: Define robotics.
points: The art, knowledge base and know-how of designing, applying and using robots

theory.q: State the Japanese definition of a robot.
points: An all-purpose machine with a memory device
That can replace human labour in the automatic performance of tasks

theory.q: Explain Schilling's definition of a robot.
points: Uses sensors to guide end effectors through programmed motions in a workspace

theory.q: Why is robotics described as interdisciplinary?
points: It combines mechanical, electrical, computing and control knowledge
All are needed to design and use a robot

points: Fixed automation does one job set by its hardware

lessons.title: Main components of an industrial robot
lessons.one_line: Arm, end effector, drive, controller, and sensors: the body, hand, muscles, brain and senses.
lessons.analogy: Body = arm, hand = end effector, muscles = drive, brain = controller, senses = sensors.
exam: Components: manipulator/arm, end effectors, drive mechanism, controller, custom features (sensors, transducers).
Five joint types: Linear (L) and Orthogonal (O) give translational motion; Rotational (R), Twisting (T) and Revolving (V) give rotary motion.
Drives: hydraulic (strong, fast, large, floor space), electric servo/stepper (accurate, repeatable, low cost, easy maintenance), pneumatic (small units, high cycle rate, easy maintenance).
End effectors attach to the wrist: grippers (mechanical, suction/vacuum, magnetic), hooks, scoops; tools (spot and arc welding, spray gun, drilling spindle, grinders, wire brushes, heating torches).
Sensors: tactile (touch, force), proximity/range (optical, acoustic, electromagnetic), miscellaneous (temperature, pressure, flow, voice), machine vision.
recall: Which is stronger for lifting a car: an air cylinder or an oil-based hydraulic ram?

quiz.q: Which joint type is 'twisting'?
quiz.explain: T = twisting (rotary). V = revolving.

quiz.q: Best drive for very heavy payloads?
quiz.explain: Hydraulic offers high strength and speed but takes floor space.

quiz.q: A suction cup is a type of:
quiz.explain: Vacuum cups are grippers.

quiz.q: Touch and force sensors are:
quiz.explain: Tactile sensors sense contact.

flashcards.back: L, O = translational; R, T, V = rotary.
Hydraulic: power, size. Electric: accuracy, low cost, clean.
Touch or force sensor.

theory.q: List the main components of an industrial robot.
points: Custom features such as sensors and transducers

theory.q: Name the five robot joint types and say which move by sliding and which rotate.
Compare hydraulic, electric and pneumatic drives.
points: Hydraulic: strong and fast, large, needs floor space
Electric: accurate and repeatable, low cost, easy maintenance
Pneumatic: small units, high cycle rate, easy maintenance

theory.q: What is an end effector? Give examples.
points: Attached to the wrist at the end of the arm
Does the task: grippers or tools
Examples: mechanical gripper, vacuum cup, welding torch

theory.q: List three types of gripper.
points: Magnetic gripper (hooks and scoops also used)

theory.q: List four tools used as end effectors.
points: Spot welding and arc welding torches
Grinders, wire brushes, heating torches (any four)

theory.q: Classify robot sensors, with examples.
points: Proximity or range: optical, acoustic, electromagnetic

theory.q: Which joints give translational motion and which give rotary motion?
points: R, T and V are rotary
Translational joints slide, rotary joints turn

lessons.title: Classifying robots (overview and control of movement)
lessons.one_line: Robots are grouped by body, how they move, geometry, power source, authority definitions, use, technology level, design, job and degrees of freedom.
lessons.analogy: Like classifying vehicles: by size, engine, purpose, owner.
exam: Ten schemes: anatomy, control of movement, kinematics/geometry, energy source, authority body, industrial/non-industrial, technology level, design, application/job, degrees of freedom.
Anatomy: arm, two-arm, arm and leg, arm/leg/face; fingers (2, 3, 5).
Limited sequence: mechanical stops and limit switches, repeatability about +/-0.5 mm, cheap (25-50% less), used in casting and pressing; hard to change stop points.
Point to point: axes stop at any programmed discrete point; used in spot welding, pick-and-place, loading and unloading.
Continuous path: moves smoothly in any direction in 3-D, position and tool controlled continuously; paint spraying, welding.
recall: When painting a car, would you want the robot to stop at points or move smoothly?

quiz.q: Which robot uses mechanical stops and limit switches?
quiz.explain: It is the simplest and cheapest type.

quiz.q: Paint spraying needs:
quiz.explain: The path itself matters, so control must be continuous.

quiz.q: Spot welding is typically:
quiz.explain: The tool visits discrete points.

flashcards.back: Limited sequence, point to point, continuous path.
About +/-0.5 mm (per the lecture).

theory.q: List the ten ways of classifying robots.
Describe the limited sequence robot with its advantages and disadvantages.
points: Movement is limited to linear direction, using mechanical stops and limit switches
Advantage: cheap, and used in casting and pressing
Disadvantage: control and movement are limited
Difficult to change stop points, longer set-up time

theory.q: Explain the point-to-point robot and give applications.
points: Axes can stop at any programmed discrete point in the workspace
No control of the path between points
Spot welding, pick and place, loading and unloading

theory.q: Explain the continuous path robot and give applications.
points: Moves in any direction continuously in 3-D space
Position and tool are controlled continuously

theory.q: Compare point-to-point and continuous path robots.
points: Point to point stops at programmed points; continuous path follows a whole path
Path between points not controlled versus path controlled
Point to point: spot welding, pick and place

theory.q: List the classes of robot by anatomy.
points: Fingers: two, three or five (any four)

theory.q: What is repeatability, and what value is given for limited sequence robots?
points: How closely a robot returns to the same position

theory.q: Which control type suits spot welding and which suits paint spraying, and why?
points: Spot welding: point to point, because only discrete points matter
Paint spraying: continuous path, because the path itself matters
Continuous path controls position and tool continuously

lessons.title: Robot configurations (coordinate systems)
lessons.one_line: The mix of joint types decides the shape of the space a robot can reach: Cartesian, cylindrical, spherical, articulated and SCARA.
lessons.analogy: A gantry crane (Cartesian), a lathe-like pivot (cylindrical), a turret (spherical), a human arm (articulated), a desk-lamp swing arm (SCARA).
exam: Workspace: the space the robot can move in.
Notation A (P/R): Cartesian PPP, Cylindrical RPP, Spherical RRP, SCARA RRP, Articulated RRR.
Notation B (L/O/R/T/V): Cartesian LOO, Cylindrical TLO, Spherical TRL, Articulated TRR, SCARA VRO.
Cartesian: three sliding joints, also called rectilinear or x-y-z robot.
Cylindrical: vertical column with an arm that moves up/down and in/out.
Spherical: sliding arm that rotates about vertical and horizontal axes.
Articulated: jointed arm, like a human arm.
SCARA: Selective Compliance Assembly (or Articulated) Robot Arm; vertical axes for shoulder and elbow, compliant horizontally, rigid vertically; suits vertical insertion.
Wrist: orients the end effector using roll, pitch and yaw (2 or 3 DOF); the body and arm set the global position.
recall: Which everyday machine has three straight-line axes?

quiz.q: PPP notation belongs to:
quiz.explain: Three prismatic (sliding) joints.

quiz.q: Which robot is most like a human arm?
quiz.explain: Articulated uses rotary joints like shoulder, elbow, wrist.

quiz.q: SCARA is compliant in the ___ direction.
quiz.explain: Compliant horizontally, rigid vertically, ideal for vertical insertion.

quiz.q: Wrist motions are:
quiz.explain: Those orient the end effector.

flashcards.back: Rectilinear, x-y-z, gantry.
Two vertical rotary axes for x-y plane compliance, rigid in z; great for assembly.
Orients the end effector; the arm positions it.

theory.q: Define workspace.
points: The space the robot can reach or move within
Set by joint types and link lengths

theory.q: List five robot configurations.
Describe the Cartesian robot.
points: Three sliding joints, two of them orthogonal
Also called rectilinear or x-y-z robot

theory.q: Describe the cylindrical robot.
points: A vertical column with an arm
The arm moves up and down and in and out

theory.q: Describe the spherical robot.
points: A sliding arm that rotates about a vertical axis and a horizontal axis

theory.q: Describe the articulated robot.
points: Jointed arm like a human arm

theory.q: What is a SCARA robot and why is it suited to assembly?
points: Selective Compliance Assembly Robot Arm (Articulated also used)
Vertical axes for shoulder and elbow

theory.q: Describe the robot wrist and its motions.
points: Attached to the end of the arm; the end effector is attached to the wrist
Orients the end effector: roll, pitch and yaw
Two or three degrees of freedom

lessons.title: Classification by energy source
lessons.one_line: What powers the joints: electricity, oil pressure, air pressure or mechanics.
lessons.analogy: Battery drill, hydraulic jack, tyre-pump air tool.
exam: Four categories: electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic, mechanical.
Electrical: DC stepper, DC servo or AC servo motors; very popular, low price, clean, silent, easy to control or brake.
Hydraulic: more powerful and faster response than electric; huge payloads; less clean, which matters in assembly.
Pneumatic: cheaper and simpler, harder to control, less dynamic; both electric and hydraulic robots commonly use pneumatic end tools.
recall: Why would oil leaks matter in a food factory?

quiz.q: Which is cleanest and quietest?
quiz.explain: Electric robots are clean, silent, popular.

quiz.q: Huge payload capacity suggests:
quiz.explain: Hydraulic offers greater power.

quiz.q: Weakness of pneumatic robots?
quiz.explain: Air compressibility makes precise control difficult.

flashcards.back: Electrical, hydraulic, pneumatic, mechanical.
Cheap, simple; hard to control, less dynamic.

theory.q: List the four categories of robot by energy source.
State the features of electrical robots.
points: Use DC stepper, DC servo or AC servo motors
Easy to assemble, control and brake

theory.q: State the features of hydraulic robots.
points: Use hydraulic energy to move the actuator
More powerful and faster response than electric

theory.q: State the features of pneumatic robots.
Compare electrical and hydraulic robots.
points: Hydraulic: less clean, which matters in assembly

theory.q: Why do electric and hydraulic robots still use pneumatic end tools?
points: Both usually use the end tool from pneumatic power
Pneumatic tools are cheap and simple

theory.q: Name the motors used in electrical robots.
Why is cleanliness a disadvantage for hydraulic robots in assembly?
points: Cleanliness is an important feature in assembling applications

lessons.title: Classification by authority body (JIRA, RIA, AFR)
lessons.one_line: Different organisations rank robots by how smart and programmable they are.
lessons.analogy: Like exam grading scales: different schools use different scales for the same students.
exam: JIRA (Japan) has 6 classes: 1 manual handling device, 2 fixed sequence, 3 variable sequence, 4 playback, 5 numerical control, 6 intelligent.
RIA (USA) considers only JIRA classes 3-6 as robots (variable sequence, playback, numerical control, intelligent).
AFR (France) has 4 types: A manual to telerobotics, B automatic handling with predetermined cycles, C programmable servo with continuous or point-to-point paths, D like C plus environment sensing.
Playback: a human teaches by demonstration. Numerical control: operator supplies the sequence. Intelligent: understands the environment and adapts.
recall: Which is smarter: a robot taught by demonstration or one that adapts by itself?

quiz.q: How many JIRA classes exist?
quiz.explain: Six, from manual handling to intelligent.

quiz.q: Which classes does RIA count as robots?
quiz.explain: RIA considers JIRA classes 3 to 6.

quiz.q: Playback robot means:
quiz.explain: The human performs the task manually to teach the trajectory.

flashcards.back: Intelligent robot.
A manual, B automatic cycles, C programmable servo, D C plus sensing.
Learns a path by a human demonstrating it.

theory.q: State the six JIRA classes.
Which JIRA classes does RIA count as robots?
points: Variable sequence, playback, numerical control, intelligent
RIA divides robots into four classes

theory.q: State the four AFR types.
points: B: automatic handling with predetermined cycles
C: programmable servo, continuous or point-to-point paths
D: like C, with the ability to sense the environment

theory.q: Describe a playback robot.
points: A human performs the task manually to teach the trajectory

theory.q: Compare the numerical control robot with the playback robot.
points: Playback: a human teaches by demonstrating the motion
Numerical control: the operator supplies the sequence of tasks
Numerical control does not need to be taught by demonstration

theory.q: Describe an intelligent robot.
points: Can successfully complete a task despite changes in surrounding conditions

theory.q: Describe a variable sequence robot.
Compare JIRA class 2 and class 3.
points: Class 2, fixed sequence: similar to fixed automation
Class 3, variable sequence: similar to programmable automation
RIA counts class 3 but not class 2 as a robot

lessons.title: Industrial vs non-industrial robots
lessons.one_line: Industrial robots work in factories on hot, heavy, hazardous jobs; non-industrial robots serve homes, schools, medicine, the military and hobbies.
lessons.analogy: A factory welding arm vs a home vacuum robot.
exam: Non-industrial: home, school, field, personal, education, army, medical, hobby, showcase. Examples: micro flying copter, ASIMO.
Industrial: manufacturing, welding, cutting, forming, assembling, heavy work, painting.
Early industrial uses: materials handling, spot welding, spray painting; jobs that were hot, heavy and hazardous (die casting, forging).
Industrial robots' key subsystems: kinematics, control system and drivers.
recall: Why were robots first sent to hot, heavy and hazardous jobs?

quiz.q: Which was an early industrial robot job?
quiz.explain: Materials handling, spot welding, spray painting.

quiz.q: ASIMO is a:
quiz.explain: It is a humanoid, non-industrial example.

flashcards.back: Materials handling, spot welding, spray painting.
Kinematics, control system, drivers.

theory.q: Distinguish industrial robots from non-industrial robots.
points: Industrial: manufacturing, welding, cutting, forming, assembling, painting
Non-industrial: home, school, medical, army, hobby
Industrial robots handle heavy, hot or hazardous factory work
Non-industrial robots serve people outside the production line

theory.q: List five areas where non-industrial robots are used.
Give two examples of non-industrial robots.
List five industrial robot applications.
State the early industrial uses of robots.
Why were robots first used on hot, heavy and hazardous jobs?
points: Such jobs are dangerous and tiring for people

theory.q: List the key subsystems of an industrial robot.
Classify a home vacuum robot and an automobile welding robot.
points: Reason: place of use and task

mechatronics.plain: Designing machines so mechanical parts, electronics and software are planned together.
mechatronics.exam: A methodology for optimal design of electromechanical products, integrating mechanical, electrical, computer science and IT.

methodology.plain: A set of agreed ways of doing something.
methodology.exam: A collection of practices, procedures and rules used in a discipline.

concurrent-design.plain: Everyone works on their part at the same time and shares information as they go.
concurrent-design.exam: Designing all disciplines in parallel rather than sequentially.

synergy.plain: When teamwork gives a better result than the parts alone.
synergy.exam: Combined effect greater than the sum of separate contributions.

multidisciplinary.exam: Embodies electrical, mechanical, computer science and IT.

modelling.plain: Drawing a simplified version of a system on a computer.
modelling.exam: Block-diagram or visual creation of behavioural models of physical or abstract phenomena.

simulation.plain: Running the model to see how it behaves.
simulation.exam: Numerical solution of models with differential, discrete, hybrid, partial and nonlinear equations.

hil.plain: Testing with a mix of real parts and virtual ones.
hil.exam: Replacing part of the model with real hardware via sensors and actuators in real time.

rapid-prototyping.plain: Quickly building a working test version.
rapid-prototyping.exam: Another name for hardware-in-the-loop use of real-time interfaces.

code-generator.plain: Software that writes program code from your diagram.
code-generator.exam: Produces efficient high-level source (usually C) from the block diagram.

embedded-processor.plain: A small computer hidden inside a product.
embedded-processor.exam: Processor that resides in the final product and communicates with the prototyping environment.

monte-carlo.plain: Testing many random variations to see what could happen.
monte-carlo.exam: Statistical simulation capability for design under variation.

life-cycle.plain: Everything from making a product to throwing it away.
life-cycle.exam: Delivery, reliability, maintainability, serviceability, upgradeability, disposability.

maintainability.plain: How easy it is to keep working.

serviceability.plain: How easy it is to find and fix a fault.
serviceability.exam: On-board diagnostics, prognostics and modular design.

modular-design.exam: Design in independent modules for easy replacement and maintenance.

specification.plain: A written list of what the product must do.
specification.exam: Statements about mass, dimensions, accuracy, I/O, power, environment, standards, etc.

conceptualisation.plain: Coming up with many possible ideas.
conceptualisation.exam: Generating possible solutions for each function (at least six).

optimisation.plain: Picking the best of your ideas.
optimisation.exam: Selecting the best solution among a group after evaluation.

detail-design.plain: Working out exact sizes, layout and parts.
detail-design.exam: Development of the chosen solution, prototype, layout and accessibility check.

tolerance.plain: How much a size is allowed to vary.
tolerance.exam: Permitted manufacturing deviation stated in working drawings.

prototype.exam: Preliminary model used to verify the design.

feedback.plain: The machine checks its own result and corrects itself.
feedback.exam: Measured output returned to the controller so accuracy is achieved by correction.

synchronisation.plain: Making several motions happen in step.

variable-speed-drive.plain: A motor whose speed can be changed on demand.
variable-speed-drive.exam: A mechatronic feature versus traditional constant-speed drives.

sensor.plain: A device that measures something and turns it into a signal.
sensor.exam: Input element sensing internal or external states.

end-effector.exam: Device attached to the robot's wrist to do a specific task.

actuator.plain: The part that makes something move.
actuator.exam: Motor, cylinder or similar driver of a joint.

solenoid-valve.plain: An electrically operated tap for air or oil.
solenoid-valve.exam: Valve switched by a solenoid to direct fluid to a cylinder.

limit-switch.plain: A switch that clicks when a part reaches a set position.

microcontroller.plain: A tiny computer on a chip with inputs and outputs.
microcontroller.exam: Controller that reads inputs and drives outputs by program.

opto-isolator.plain: Uses light to pass a signal so circuits stay electrically separate.
opto-isolator.exam: LED plus light-sensitive switch giving electrical isolation.

triac.plain: An electronic switch for AC power.
triac.exam: Bidirectional thyristor used to switch AC loads.

hydraulic.exam: High force and speed; large; less clean.

ecu.exam: Engine Control Unit governing fuelling and ignition.

adc.plain: Turns a smooth signal into numbers.

dac.plain: Turns numbers into a smooth signal.

set-point.plain: The target value the controller aims for.
set-point.exam: Stored reference value compared to measured input.

signal-conditioning.plain: Cleaning and scaling a signal so the controller can use it.
signal-conditioning.exam: Amplifying, filtering and level-shifting a sensor signal.

thermistor.plain: A resistor whose resistance changes with temperature.
thermistor.exam: Temperature-sensitive resistor used as a temperature sensor.

hot-wire-anemometer.plain: A heated wire that cools as air flows past it.
hot-wire-anemometer.exam: Mass airflow sensor; cooling depends on mass flow rate.

oxygen-sensor.plain: Measures how much oxygen is left in exhaust.
oxygen-sensor.exam: Zirconia tube with platinum electrodes; generates voltage above ~300 C.

ignition-timing.exam: Timing of high-voltage pulses relative to crankshaft position.

plc.plain: A rugged industrial computer for machines.
plc.exam: Programmable Logic Controller with input and output modules.

solenoid.plain: A coil that becomes a magnet when current flows.
solenoid.exam: Electromagnet used to move a plunger or valve.

piston-cylinder.plain: A rod pushed in and out by pressure.
piston-cylinder.exam: Linear actuator driven by fluid pressure.

automation.plain: Machines doing the job with little human help.
automation.exam: Process to create, control and monitor technology with minimum human effort.

productivity.plain: Output per worker or per hour.
productivity.exam: Labour productivity is one motivation for automation.

lead-time.plain: Time from starting to finishing a product.
lead-time.exam: Manufacturing lead time, reduced by automation.

fixed-automation.plain: A machine built for one job.
fixed-automation.exam: Hardware-based, inflexible, highest efficiency at high volume.

programmable-automation.plain: Same machine, new program for a new batch.
programmable-automation.exam: Hardware plus software; batch production; set-up time between batches.

flexible-automation.plain: Change products with almost no stopping.
flexible-automation.exam: Also FMS/CIM; several products at once.

fms.plain: A factory system that can switch between products smoothly.

cim.plain: Computers linking design, planning and production.

batch-production.plain: Making a group of the same product, then switching.
batch-production.exam: Production in batches, suits programmable automation.

robot.plain: A reprogrammable machine that moves things automatically.

robotics.plain: The study and use of robots.
robotics.exam: Interdisciplinary art and know-how of designing, applying and using robots.

manipulator.plain: The arm part of a robot.
manipulator.exam: Series of links connected by joints with actuators.

joint.plain: Where two links meet and move.

ria.exam: Robotics Industry (or Institute of) America; note the slides use both names.

machine-vision.exam: Vision systems for inspection and guidance.

servo-motor.plain: A motor with feedback for exact position.
servo-motor.exam: Motor with position feedback, accurate and repeatable.

stepper-motor.plain: A motor that turns in small fixed steps.
stepper-motor.exam: Moves in discrete steps, accurate positioning.

limited-sequence.exam: Mechanical stops and limit switches, repeatability about 0.5 mm.

point-to-point.exam: Stops at programmed discrete points; spot welding, pick-and-place.

continuous-path.plain: Moves smoothly along a whole path.
continuous-path.exam: Controls position and tool continuously in 3-D; paint spraying.

dof.plain: Number of independent ways it can move.
dof.exam: DOF of joints and wrist (2 or 3 for a wrist).

repeatability.plain: How closely it returns to the same spot.
repeatability.exam: Tolerance of returning to a taught position.

cartesian-robot.plain: Moves in straight x, y, z lines.
cartesian-robot.exam: Three sliding joints; rectilinear; PPP or LOO.

cylindrical-robot.exam: Vertical column with arm; RPP or TLO.

spherical-robot.plain: Pivots and extends like a turret.
spherical-robot.exam: Sliding arm on rotating body; RRP or TRL.

scara.plain: A robot arm stiff up-down but flexible sideways.

workspace.plain: The space the robot can reach.
workspace.exam: Space the manipulator can move within.

wrist.plain: The joint group that turns the hand.
wrist.exam: Orients the end effector with roll, pitch and yaw.

afr.exam: Association Francaise de Robotique, types A-D.

playback-robot.plain: Repeats a motion a human showed it.

industrial-robot.exam: Robot used in manufacturing, welding, cutting, assembling, painting.
